query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy nanoalloys for high‐temperature applications, structural and chemical stability is maintained because the very high configurational entropy at elevated temperatures suppresses the enthalpically driven local ordering (or clustering) tendencies, especially when high-melting refractory elements are present. This dominant entropy stabilization (reflected in a disordered single-phase, typically BCC, structure) overcomes the chemical pair‐interaction forces that might otherwise promote phase separation or ordering at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy nanoalloy with near-equiatomic ratios of refractory elements (e.g., a BCC-structured alloy containing elements such as Cr, Co, Fe, Ni with minor additions of Al or other high-melting components) in a disordered solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Heat treatment (annealing) at temperatures close to the alloy’s operational regime (near 0.8–0.95 Tm) under controlled atmospheres.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions without applied tensile stress, compared to a control sample annealed at lower temperatures or with reduced refractory element content.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of short-range chemical order vs. complete disorder in the atomic lattice (e.g., retention of a homogeneous BCC phase versus the appearance of ordered clusters).
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures the configurational entropy is maximized, which statistically favors a uniform solid solution by offsetting the pairwise chemical interactions that would normally drive clustering or ordering. The inclusion of high-melting refractory elements further elevates the melting point and stabilizes the high-entropy phase, ensuring that the entropic contribution dominates even in nanoalloy forms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoalloy samples treated at high temperatures will maintain a single-phase disordered (e.g., BCC) structure with minimal local ordering, while similar alloys with lower refractory content or those annealed at lower temperatures will show increased signatures of chemical ordering or phase separation.
generation.baseline: A comparable nanoalloy either with reduced refractory element content or heat treated at lower temperatures (below the threshold where configurational entropy dominates).
generation.boundary: This prediction applies in the high-temperature regime (roughly 80–95% of the melting temperature), under conditions free from significant mechanical stress; deviations may occur if temperatures drop below this range or if external stresses induce ordering transitions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative crossover point between entropy-dominated stabilization and enthalpy-driven ordering, as well as the effects of minor compositional variations and mechanical loading conditions, are not precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples: one set with high refractory element content and another set with reduced refractory content. Subject both sets to high-temperature annealing near 0.8–0.95 Tm in identical, controlled atmospheric conditions. Use a parallel group annealed at a lower temperature to serve as a baseline. Characterize the phases using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the degree of chemical disorder vs. ordering.
measurements: XRD peak positions and breadths (to identify single-phase vs. multiphase structure)
TEM imaging and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) to detect any local chemical clustering or ordering
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess phase-transition temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high refractory content samples annealed at high temperature exhibit significant local chemical ordering, phase separation, or a multiphase structure comparable to or worse than the low refractory content samples, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy (enhanced by refractory elements) governs stability under high temperatures is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To search for potentially stable single-phase HEAs and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying their phase stability, we have navigated the vast chemical space of all quinary equimolar alloys from the combinations of 40 elements using our model. Among the 658,008 quinary alloys, we predict that 5% of them can be stabilized in a single-phase solid solution at near-melting point. The amount of predicted equimolar HEAs corresponds to the theoretical upper limit, and is significantly more than what has been reported in the literature. The predicted HEAs show a strong tendency to form BCC phases, in line with the large body of BCC HEAs that have already been identified. Our model suggests that the prevailing BCC phase originates from a combined effect of the high melting of the constituent BCC elements, which are often refractory, and a favorable mixing of elements on a BCC lattice. The high melting point is in fact one of the main driving forces for the single-phase HEA formation. By that token, many closed-packed alloys, such as the FCC Cantor alloy, are more the exception than the rule as they normally contain zero to very few refractory elements.

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The RBA scheme is successful in predicting the presence of complex Sigma phase in the previously unreported CoFN-Vx composition (n ≤ 7.6) and allows the prediction of other complex intermetallic phases in various new alloy compositions as a function of n. A design strategy based on this approach would be that through a careful selection of elements and/or utilising a known HEA composition with high n as a ‘base’ phase (FCC), it would be possible to include elements of interest for purposes such as corrosion resistance, biocompatibility, and high-temperature resistance, while mechanical properties could be influenced by changing the phase fraction and composition.
